title: Spelling-change verbs
topic: -er verbs with stem changes: acheter, préférer, appeler, manger, commencer, payer
why: These -er verbs have regular endings but a stem that changes its spelling: j'achète, je préfère, j'appelle, nous mangeons, nous commençons, je paie. Once you understand the sound behind the boot pattern, you'll spell them right, and talk about preferences, shopping and food.

The boot: è and double consonants

Some -er verbs have perfectly regular endings but a stem whose spelling changes. The reason is pronunciation. When the ending is silent (-e, -es, -e, -ent), the last vowel of the stem is stressed and becomes an open “è” sound, which French writes with a grave accent or a double consonant. With nous and vous, the ending is pronounced, so the stem stays as in the infinitive. Draw a line around the forms that change and you get the shape of a boot.

acheterpréférerappeler
je (j')achètepréfèreappelle
tuachètespréfèresappelles
il, elle, onachètepréfèreappelle
nousachetonspréféronsappelons
vousachetezpréférezappelez
ils, ellesachètentpréfèrentappellent
  • e → è: acheter (to buy), se lever (je me lève: you already know it), se promener (to go for a walk).
  • é → è: préférer (to prefer), espérer (to hope), répéter (to repeat). Only the second accent changes: je préfère.
  • double consonant: appeler (to call), jeter (to throw away): je jette, nous jetons.
Je préfère la mer, mais nous préférons la montagne.I prefer the sea, but we prefer the mountains.

Now you can understand je m'appelle: it's appeler, “to call oneself”. That's why it has two l's, while nous nous appelons has only one.

-ger, -cer and -yer

Here the change only affects nous, and it's purely a matter of spelling. Before -ons, a g would sound hard (as in “go”) and a c would sound like a k. So French adds an e after the g and puts a cedilla under the c, to keep the soft sound of the infinitive.

mangercommencerpayer
jemangecommencepaie
tumangescommencespaies
il, elle, onmangecommencepaie
nousmangeonscommençonspayons
vousmangezcommencezpayez
ils, ellesmangentcommencentpaient
  • Like manger: voyager (to travel), nager (to swim), partager (to share): nous voyageons, nous nageons, nous partageons.
  • Like commencer: avancer (to move forward), prononcer (to pronounce): nous prononçons.
  • -yer verbs change y to i before a silent ending: payer (je paie), envoyer (j'envoie, to send), essayer (j'essaie, to try). With payer and essayer, je paye and j'essaye are also correct.
Nous commençons à huit heures et nous mangeons à midi.We start at eight and we eat at noon.

“To pay for something” has no preposition in French: Je paie le café (I'm paying for the coffee). English speakers often add pour, which changes the meaning: payer pour Léa means paying instead of Léa, on her behalf.

", "

Preferences, shopping, food

These verbs are everywhere when you talk about what you like and what you buy. Here are some sentences to learn as they are:

FrenchEnglish
Tu préfères le thé ou le café ?Do you prefer tea or coffee?
J'achète une baguette le matin.I buy a baguette in the morning.
On mange à quelle heure ?What time are we eating?
Vous payez par carte ?Are you paying by card?
J'essaie la robe.I'm trying on the dress.
J'appelle Léa ce soir.I'm calling Léa tonight.
J'espère que tu vas bien.I hope you're well.
Vous pouvez répéter ?Can you repeat that?

Like aimer, préférer takes le, la, les when you talk about something in general: Je préfère le poisson (I prefer fish). It can also be followed by an infinitive: Je préfère rester ici (I'd rather stay here). To pay, you'll hear par carte (by card) or en espèces (in cash).

The best way to remember all these changes is to say the forms aloud. If you hear an open “è” at the end of the stem, there's an accent or a double consonant: j'achète, j'appelle. If you don't, there isn't: nous achetons, nous appelons.
